Abstract:
The bulk properties of powders depend on material characteristics and size of the primary particles. During storage and transportation processes in the powder processing industry, the material undergoes various modes of deformation and stress conditions, e.g., due to compression or shear. In many applications, it is important to know when powders are yielding, i.e. when they start to flow under shear; in other cases it is necessary to know how much stress is needed to keep them flowing. The measurement of powder yield and flow properties is still a challenge and will be addressed in this study. In the framework of the collaborative project T-MAPPP, a large set of shear experiments using different shear devices, namely the Jenike shear tester, the ELE direct shear tester, the Schulze ring shear tester and the FT4 powder rheometer, have been carried out on eight chemically-identical limestone powders of different particle sizes in a wide range of confining stresses. These experiments serve two goals: i) to test the reproducibility/consistency among different shear devices and testing protocols; ii) to relate the bulk behaviour to microscopic particle properties, focusing on the effect of particle size and thus inter-particle cohesion. The experiments show high repeatability for all shear devices, though some of them show more fluctuations than others. All devices provide consistent results, where the FT4 powder rheometer gives lower yield/steady state stress values, due to a different pre-shearing protocol. As expected, the bulk cohesion decreases with increasing particle size (up to 150 μm), due to the decrease of inter-particle cohesion. The bulk friction, characterized in different ways, is following a similar decreasing trend, whereas the bulk density increases with particle size in this range. Interestingly, for samples with particle sizes larger than 150 μm, the bulk cohesion increases slightly, while the bulk friction increases considerably—presumably due to particle interlocking effects—up to magnitudes comparable to those of the finest powders. Furthermore, removing the fines from the coarse powder samples reduces the bulk cohesion and bulk density, but has a negligible effect on the bulk friction. In addition to providing useful insights into the role of microscopically attractive, van der Waals, gravitational and/or compressive forces for the macroscopic bulk powder flow behaviour, the experimental data provide a robust database of cohesive and frictional fine powders for industrially relevant designs such as silos, as well as for calibration and validation of models and computer simulations.

Abstract:
<jats:p><p dir="ltr">Particle mixing is a critical process in industries dealing with powders, such as pharmaceuticals and chemicals. However, understanding the complex mechanisms governing particle behavior during mixing is a significant challenge. The nonlinear nature of particle flow makes it difficult to precisely understand particle interactions. Traditional experimental methods often fall short in providing a comprehensive understanding of these intricate behaviors due to complex flow patterns and limitations in measurement techniques. To address these challenges, numerical simulations have emerged as a powerful tool, facilitated by advancements in computer technology. They offer both microscopic and macroscopic insights into particulate materials that are challenging to obtain through experiments alone. In practical industrial systems, convective mixers and twin paddle blenders are commonly utilized. Twin paddle blenders offer advantages in terms of material loading and cleaning and are suitable for a wide range of capacities. However, research on these specific mixers has been limited, and additional complexity arises from restrictions in investigating non-spherical particles and cohesive materials. Thus, this study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by investigating powder blending in double paddle mixers, utilizing a combination of Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations and experiments.</p><p dir="ltr">The study begins by examining flow patterns and mixing mechanisms within double paddle blenders. DEM results reveal that impeller speed and initial loading patterns significantly impact mixing quality, with diffusion emerging as the primary mixing mechanism. The study delves into the role of particle characteristics, encompassing both spherical and non-spherical particles, and their influence on mixing behavior. Furthermore, it investigates the impact of mixer design parameters, such as paddle angle, width, and gap, on mixing quality, assessed through metrics like relative standard deviation (RSD) and power consumption. Moreover, the thesis addresses the calibration of DEM input parameters, with a particular focus on cohesive materials. It compares various models and identifies the Random Forest model as a means to enhance the accuracy and reliability of DEM simulations for cohesive materials. The thesis concludes by investigating the correlation between DEM results and operational parameters using machine learning techniques, providing comprehensive insight into granular mixing behaviors and their connection to operational variables.</p></jats:p>

The excerpt documents Lu et al.’s controlled-humidity lactose experiment: coarse/fine lactose blends were conditioned for 48 h at 0%, 30%, 58%, and 85% RH, at 25 ± 1 °C. It reports qualitative caking at 85% RH and describes RH-dependent changes in flowability and dispersion, including deterioration at 85% RH and improvement after conditioning at 58% RH. The FT4 Powder Rheometer measurements included dynamic, permeability, and shear-cell tests, with measurements repeated three times. The Hird and Bolton excerpt documents autogenous wicking of sodium chloride from a brine pool through dry porous materials. The only explicit numerical humidity value here is a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of approximately 75% for crystals larger than 1 µm; the process continues when surrounding relative humidity remains below this threshold, allowing evaporation at dendrite tips. It also states that wicking continues while the dendrite remains connected to the brine pool. Electrical conductivity established connectivity between migrating salt and its source brine. No conditioning times, mass-uptake values, hysteresis measurements, rate-dependence data, solid-bridge caking results, FT4 flow measurements, or BaCl2-specific evidence are reported in this excerpt. This excerpt documents Lu et al.’s controlled-humidity lactose experiments at 0%, 30%, 58%, and 85% relative humidity. The excerpt is relevant to evaporation-driven erosion in a partially saturated granular slope modeled with a discrete element method (DEM). The DEM includes capillary effects at inter-particle contacts through a minimum-energy approach and incorporates an evaporation-rate law dependent on depth and the air–water interface. Numerical triaxial tests reportedly show increased shear strength at low water content. The model was compared with the physical slope-drying tests and reproduced the erosion process and formation of a talus-slope profile; both experiments and simulations showed rigid displacement at the slope toe after an initial shallow-erosion phase. However, these pages do not provide a humidity-dependent Kelvin equation, a diffusion- or kinetic-based evaporation formulation, or an explicit distinction between relative humidity (RH) and pre-added liquid water. This excerpt documents MercuryDPM only; it provides no evidence about LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, or Yade, so those packages’ capillary-bridge capabilities cannot be inferred from this source. MercuryDPM implements both the classical Willett and Bagheri capillary-bridge approximations. These are exposed through species combining a normal model, friction model, and adhesive liquid-bridge model. The documented examples are HertzianViscoelasticMindlinLiquidBridgeBagheriSpecies, which combines dissipative Hertz normal force, Mindlin friction, and Bagheri liquid-bridge adhesion, and HertzianViscoelasticMindlinLiquidBridgeClassicalWilletSpecies, which substitutes the classical Willett approximation. The paper states that Bagheri’s applicability was extended to unequal particle sizes, although the approximation was originally developed for equal-radius particles. The models use contact angle, liquid-bridge volume, and separation distance, together with an effective radius for two interacting particles. Capillary forces remain active until the bridge reaches the rupture distance Sc. The excerpt also says the implementations are in MercuryDPM’s master branch and that code and test scripts are available in the cited GitHub repository. It does not document imposed suction, independently prescribed fluid volume controls beyond the bridge-volume parameter, or any limitations beyond the stated origin of the Bagheri approximation and its extension to unequal sizes.

MercuryDPM already supplied a simplified Willett approximation, available under the model name `LiquidBridgeWillet`. This work adds two further adhesive contact models: the classical Willett approximation (`LiquidBridgeClassicalWillet`) and the Bagheri approximation (`LiquidBridgeBagheri`). The paper states that the Bagheri formulation was originally developed for equal-sized spheres and is extended here to particles of unequal sizes, giving it applicability to polydisperse systems. The reported simulations use a nonlinear liquid-bridge model together with dissipative Hertz contact forces, and compare the simplified Willett, classical Willett, and Bagheri approximations. In the described setup, particles are not capillary-linked before contact; a liquid bridge forms once they contact, and the capillary force remains at the corresponding separation until bridge rupture. The excerpt also notes that Bagheri’s approximation provides liquid-bridge surface area, which is useful for evaporation modeling. These are the explicitly documented MercuryDPM facts in the supplied pages; the excerpt does not establish what the other three packages natively supply, whether they require user-added fixes, or any additional limitations beyond the stated original equal-size scope of Bagheri.

## 1. bagheri2025discreteelementsimulations pages 1-5 (Context ID: pqac-00000016)

             Discrete Element Simulations of particles interacting via
                        capillary forces using MercuryDPM

                      Meysam Bagheri∗, Sudeshna Roy, Thorsten P¨oschel

                       Institute for Multiscale Simulation, Friedrich-Alexander-Universit¨at Erlangen-N¨urnberg,
                                                    Erlangen, Germany
2024
              Abstract

           We present the implementation of two advanced capillary bridge approxima-Nov
                   tions within the Discrete Element Method (DEM) framework of the open-4
                 source code MercuryDPM. While MercuryDPM already includes a simpli-
                    fied version of the Willett approximation, our work involves implementing
               both the classical Willett approximation and the recently published Bagheri
                approximation in MercuryDPM. Through detailed descriptions and illustra-
                   tive simulations using a two-particle collision model, we demonstrate the
               enhanced accuracy and capabilities of these approximations in capturing the
               complex dynamics of wet granular matter.

                Keywords:  Discrete Element Method - DEM, liquid bridge, capillary force,[cond-mat.soft]              particle sizes


             Metadata

                  1. Motivation and significance

                    In the study of particulate systems, understanding the interactions be-
                tween particles in the presence of liquid phases is crucial for a variety of in-
                   dustrial and scientific applications [1, 2]. One of the key phenomena in such
                systems is the formation of liquid bridges between particles, which causes
                   forces due to capillarity [3].  These interactions can significantly influence
                 the mechanical properties and behavior of granular materials [4, 5, 6]. Liq-
                 uid capillary bridges play a vital role in many processes, in the fields of soilarXiv:2411.02042v1
                mechanics and powder technology [7, 8].  Accurately approximating these
                   forces is therefore essential for reliable simulations of wet granular materi-
                      als.  Incorporating these complex interactions into DEM simulations poses

significant challenges. The na¨ıve way to account for capillary forces between
particles linked with a liquid bridge (see Figure 1) would require solving the
Young-Laplace equation for the capillary force in each time step of the DEM
integration, which is certainly not feasible. Therefore, fit formulae were elab-
orated which approximate the capillary force as a function of the particle
and liquid properties. The evaluation of these fit formulae is by orders of
magnitude more efficient than the numerical solution of the Young-Laplace
equation. The fit formulae by Willett et al. [9] and Bagheri et al. [10] have
been shown to be highly accurate, where the latter delivers also the surface
area of a liquid bridge which is needed when considering evaporation pro-
cesses in wet granulate. By now, DEM packages rely on more simple and less
accurate formulae.
   The current article reports the implementation of highly accurate descrip-
tions of capillary forces in the DEM package MercuryDPM. MercuryDPM is
a versatile open-source code designed for simulating the dynamics of partic-
ulate materials using DEM [11, 12]. Its flexibility and extensibility make it
an ideal tool for simulations of large scale granular systems By enhancing
MercuryDPM with accurate liquid bridge approximations, researchers and
engineers can gain deeper insights into the behavior of wet granular systems
and improve the design and optimization of related processes.
   The Bagheri approximation, originally formulated for equal-sized spheres


                                 2        Figure 1: Capillary bridge spanning between two unequal-sized particles.


[10], is extended in this work to account for particles of unequal sizes. This
application note outlines the implementation of both the Bagheri approxima-
tion [10] and the Willett approximation [9] into MercuryDPM for modeling
liquid capillary bridges. Additionally, we compare the results with the simpli-
fied Willett approximation already integrated into MercuryDPM. This new
implementation significantly improves MercuryDPM ’s ability to predict the
behavior of wet granular materials.
   The following sections of this note describe the particle simulation system
and detail the contact models. Subsequently, we demonstrate the implemen-
tation of the codes.  Finally, we show illustrative examples and discuss the
performance and applicability of the approximations in various scenarios. A
detailed description of the different capillary force approximations is provided
in Appendix A.


2. Software description

2.1. Software architecture
   Our simulations use a two-particle collision model to analyze interac-
tions between particles of unequal radii, as shown in Figure 2. The contact
model combines dissipative Hertz contact forces [13, 14] with a non-linear
liquid bridge model for capillary forces. The results from the implementa-
tion of different liquid bridge approximations—namely, the simplified Willett
approximation, the classical Willett approximation, and the Bagheri approx-
imation—are compared. The parameters used in DEM simulations are given
in Table 1. Two different particle size ratios are considered in the two-particle
simulations: 0.5 mm and 0.8 mm, and 0.5 mm and 1 mm, respectively. When


                                 3particles approach each other at a certain distance S, they are not linked by
a liquid bridge and there is no capillary force. Once particles are in contact,
a liquid bridge forms. After contact, the capillary force, F(S), is present at
the same distance S between the particles until the bridge ruptures.

2.2. Software functionalities
   The simplified Willett approximation is available in MercuryDPM under
the name LiquidBridgeWillet. The new adhesive contact models are imple-
mented in MercuryDPM under the names LiquidBridgeBagheri and Liquid-
BridgeClassicalWillet, respectively. We compare the force versus interparticle
distance results from three liquid bridge approximations for different particle
size ratios and different liquid bridge volumes. We discuss the accuracy of

approximation for simulating polydisperse systems, even though it was orig-

        University of Groningen


       BACHELOR RESEARCH PROJECT


  Simulating Capillary Force Bridges
   Using LAMMPS in Ambient and
  Aqueous-Ambient Conditions: The
        Influence of Roughness.





Author:
Magdalena Janewska


                                                    Page count:
Supervisors:
                                                                27
Prof. G. Palasantzas
Prof. A. Grubisic-Cabo
MSc R. B. Seraji



                       July 11, 2024                              Abstract

   This study investigated the formation of capillary force bridges between two solid
silicon surfaces, due to DI water liquid meniscus (ambient) and nitrogen nanobubbles
(aqueous-ambient) under varying roughness (rms) conditions using LAMMPS molecular
dynamics simulations. The output capillary force was then compared to its corresponding
result from the theoretical models and the experimental values from other studies.
The research focused on two geometries: plane-plane (P-P) and sphere-plane (S-P).
For theoretical formulas, surface tension was measured to accurately characterize
liquid’s cohesive properties and its impact on capillary force formation.  Due to
limited time and a wrong choice of parameters, simulations of the aqueous-ambient
conditions were not performed. For ambient conditions, results indicated significant
discrepancies between simulated, theoretical, and experimental (AFM) capillary forces,
largely attributed to simulation parameter inaccuracies. Under ambient conditions,
water’s surface tension was vastly overestimated, ranging from 101 to 102 N/m,
compared to the literature value of 71.97 mN/m [1], impacting capillary force magnitudes.
Simulated capillary forces ranged from 100-101 N for plane-plane to 103 N for sphere-
plane configuration, while theoretical values were in the order of 10−6 N. Thus, both
approaches overestimated the experimental capillary forces that were in the range of
10−7 −10−9N[2]. The study found that roughness did not significantly alter capillary
forces within the tested range of 0.00 to 1.36 nm of total RMS roughness (sum of
two components), aligning with experimental (AFM) data and suggesting a threshold
roughness beyond 1.36 nm necessary for the magnitude to decrease.  Theoretical
models displayed trends partially agreeing with simulated behavior, highlighting their
limitations in providing accurate descriptions for varying roughness.  In the same
roughness range, the plane-plane geometry displayed an increasing step-like behaviour,
while the sphere-plane configuration did not show any specific trends. The results
of the study emphasize the need for refined simulation parameters and advanced
theoretical models (that focus on roughness outside of its surface tension definition) to
bridge the gap between theoretical and experimental results, providing more reliable
predictions of capillary forces in various conditions.

    I would like to express my deepest gratitude to my supervisors, Professor George
Palasantzas and Professor Antonija Grubisic-Cabo for their support and supervision
during the period of my thesis.   I would also like to thank my supervising PhD
candidate Razieh BakhshandehSeraji for invaluable guidance on the theoretical aspects
of my research. Her expertise and encouragement were instrumental in shaping this
work.

Abstract
Undesired agglomeration of powders, known as caking, results in the loss of product quality and is
unacceptable in many powder industries. Information on how ambient conditions influence the cake
strength is essential to prevent caking. Although there are a lot of existing methods to form caked
samples and even more to characterize them, there is still no consensus regarding these methods.
Repeatability is rarely evaluated and the comparative studies remain infrequent. As a deliquescent
powder, sucrose is characterized by a threshold Relative Humidity (RH), called Deliquescence Relative
Humidity (DRH), above which it turns into an aqueous solution. Partially deliquesced crystals are
linked by liquid bridges of aqueous solution. When the RH is decreased below the DRH, these liquid
bridges recrystallize into solid bridges to form a hard cake. In this study, an accelerated caking device
was developed to obtain homogeneous caked samples of sucrose under controlled conditions. Three
mechanical tests were compared on the basis of their sensitivity and repeatability: the uniaxial
compression test, the diametrical compression test (tensile test) and the shear test. The varying
parameter was the amount of water uptaken before drying, and the data were fitted by cross-
validated local linear nonparametric regression. The best mechanical test was found to be the shear
test, giving a sharp failure of the cake along a predetermined failure surface and a linear relationship
between the cake strength and the amount of water uptaken.

Graphical abstract





                                                                                1Highlights
1. Homogeneous sucrose cakes were obtained under controlled conditions in a few hours.
2. Compression, tensile and shear tests were compared.
3. The shear test gave a sharp failure of the cake along a predetermined surface.
4. The results were fitted by a cross-validated local linear regression.
5. The shear test was found to be the most sensitive and repeatable method.

Keywords
Caking; sucrose; shear test; uniaxial compression; diametrical compression; Kernel regression

1. Introduction
Good powder  flowability  is  critical  in many  industries including food, detergents,  fertilizers,
pharmaceuticals and chemicals. This property can be jeopardized during processing, handling and
storage.  In  particular, a free-flowing powder  is  likely to form lumps through an undesired
phenomenon called caking. Caking can affect the manufacturability, the quality and the shelf life of
products. The consequences are significant, leading to costly losses of product, process interruptions
and customer complaints.
Many mechanisms can be involved  in the caking phenomenon.  In order to give a better
understanding, five categories of bonds between the particles adapted from the classification
proposed by Rumpf and Schubert (1974) are distinguished (Figure 1): (a) interparticular forces (Van
der Waals, H-bonds, electrostatic interactions…), (b) mobile liquid bridge, (c) immobile liquid bridge,
(d) solid bridge and (e) entanglement. Unlike the others, the formation of solid bridges is irreversible;
it also constitutes the strongest interaction level. The most severe cases of caking usually involve
solid bridges.





                                                                                2                                      Figure 1: The five categories of particle bonds

Solid bridges can be formed through many different mechanisms, which depend on the nature of the
powder material. In the case of hydro-soluble crystalline materials, the main mechanism of solid
bridge formation  is the deliquescence phenomenon followed by recrystallization of the solute.
Deliquescence is a phase transition of a solid to its saturated solution at a well-defined Relative
Humidity (RH), i.e. the Deliquescence Relative Humidity (DRH). The DRH depends on the material’s
nature and the temperature (Mauer and Taylor, 2010). Below this characteristic threshold, the
crystal surrounded by moist air is thermodynamically stable while above the DRH, the aqueous
solution is the most stable phase (Figure 2).





                      Figure 2: Deliquescence phenomenon (adapted from Mauer and Taylor (2010))

When the crystals undergo a partial deliquescence, they are then surrounded by a layer of aqueous
solution forming a liquid bridge between them. If the deliquescence continues, the crystals undergo
a complete dissolution followed by the dilution of the aqueous solution. The reverse process of
deliquescence is called efflorescence, which corresponds to the crystallization of a solid combined
with water evaporation. When partially deliquesced crystals are submitted to a RH below the DRH,
efflorescence occurs and liquid bridges recrystallize into solid bridges (Figure 3).





                                       Figure 3: Mechanism of crystalline caking

The mechanical resistance of these bridges depends on the environmental conditions (temperature,
RH, stresses) and on the hydro-soluble crystals’ properties (solubility, shape, particle size).
Among the wide  variety  of deliquescent powders, a model material  representative  of  this
deliquescence-efflorescence mechanism was chosen for this study: sucrose, characterized by a DRH

                                                                                3of 85% at 25° C (Mauer and Taylor, 2010). Due to its sweetening power and its conservation
properties, it is one of the most common and widely used sugars in the food and pharmaceutical
industries (Edrisi Sormoli et al., 2013).
In order to prevent caking, a better understanding of the risk factors and their influence on the
resistance of the solid bridges is required. Consequently, in the literature, a large number of methods
have been developed to reproduce and to characterize caking. In this study, an attempt to obtain
homogeneous caked samples in a relatively short amount of time and in controlled conditions of
humidity, temperature and stress is presented. To characterize the mechanical properties of the
cakes thus obtained, many tests have been proposed. However, few studies actually compared those
tests and there is no established and generally admitted characterization method so far. Thus, this
work presents a comparison of three mechanical tests, selected from the literature, on the basis of
two criteria: sensitiv

polymorphic transform would not happen at room temperature during these experiments. Thus,
the impact of the conversion between the two forms was small and was ignored. At elevated RH,

may exchange with the free water in the environment [25,26]. Above an RH of 65% in the air, capillary

RH is below 65%, the inter-particle force is mainly dominated by the Lifshitz-van der Waals force and

URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10035-013-0430-z, doi:10.1007/s10035-013-0430-z. This article has 65 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The Schwarze et al. (2013) excerpt documents a wet-capillary-bridge implementation in LIGGGHTS 2.3.2. Each bridge is characterized by its liquid volume Vb, surface distance s, particle radius R, contact angle θ, and liquid surface tension γ. The capillary force follows the Willett et al. gorge-method approximation, with the excerpt displaying a force proportional to 2πγR cos(θ) and dependent on the dimensionless separation s√(R/Vb). The bridge force remains active during and after mechanical contact, until the separation exceeds a critical rupture distance scrit; it then becomes zero. The model validation used equal particles, a surface tension of 20.6 mN/m, and several prescribed bridge volumes. The excerpt does not describe a liquid-transfer or redistribution model between contacts, so mass conservation of liquid across multiple bridges cannot be established from this text. It likewise does not identify a separate capillary-viscosity law: the listed normal and tangential viscous coefficients belong to mechanical contact damping, while γ represents surface tension rather than viscosity. LIGGGHTS implementation status is explicitly stated as an open-source DEM implementation, version 2.3.2. No humidity field, ambient-relative-humidity coupling, evaporation, or humidity simulation is mentioned in the excerpt. Evidence from Kumar (2021) would be required for claims beyond these points.

This excerpt from Schwarze et al. (2013) concerns LIGGGHTS-DEM simulations of weakly wetted granular materials, but it does not provide implementation-level details for a liquid-transfer model, capillary-force equations, viscosity laws, mass conservation, source-code availability, or humidity simulation. It states that wet simulations include liquid bridges characterized by bridge volume Vb and contact angle θ, with examples Vb = 4.2 nl and 42 nl and θ = 0° or 20°. Liquid-bridge forces increase shear-stress magnitudes and shift the macroscopic yield-stress locus upward; wet data are fitted using a cohesion offset c, illustrated with c = 5 Pa. The study reports that adding small liquid amounts increases apparent viscosity by approximately 10–20%, while the viscosity scaling with inertial number changes between regimes, from η ∼ I^−0.9 to η ∼ I^−2. Wetting also modifies shear-band position and width: increasing liquid content moves the center inward, initially narrows the band at small liquid content, and broadens it at larger content. The excerpt explicitly verifies the basic LIGGGHTS code and dry contact-model implementation, but this does not establish the status of wet-capillary source code. No humidity variable or humidity-driven liquid-equilibration process is described. Kumar (2021) is not included in the supplied excerpt, so no claims about its implementation can be extracted here.

## pqac-00000027

From text 'kumar2021particlescalemodelingto pages 4-5'.

Ashish Kumar, Stefan Radl, Krist V. Gernaey, Thomas De Beer, and Ingmar Nopens. Particle-scale modeling to understand liquid distribution in twin-screw wet granulation. Pharmaceutics, 13:928, Jun 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics13070928, doi:10.3390/pharmaceutics13070928. This article has 20 citations.

Kumar et al. (2021) describe a particle-scale wet capillary-bridge implementation in which cohesive forces are calculated with the Mikami et al. capillary-force model, while liquid distribution during bridge formation is tracked using model C of Mohan et al. When wetted particles contact, a fraction of the surface liquid, φtr, is exchanged at a finite transfer rate Qtr. The transfer timescale tref depends on the effective radius, liquid viscosity μl, and liquid surface tension σl, so viscosity enters the transfer kinetics through tref = reff μl/σl. The transferred fraction is determined from particle radii, and the steady bridge volume is calculated from the liquid contents of the two particles and φtr. The article tracks per-particle liquid content, bridge volumes, liquid bridges, and particle contacts; it also defines a global liquid-bridge fraction as the sum of bridge volumes divided by total liquid (bridge plus particle-surface liquid), which provides a mass-accounting measure. However, this excerpt does not identify the exact LIGGGHTS source implementation, its availability/status, or whether humidity is simulated. It also does not provide the detailed capillary-force equation or explicitly state a separate mass-conservation algorithm. Information from Schwarze (2013) is not included in the supplied excerpt, so source-status and humidity conclusions cannot be established here.

## pqac-00000028

From text 'rhea2018multiphaseflowin pages 27-32'.

C Rhea. Multiphase flow in a hele-shaw cell. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt describes a wet-particle implementation conceptually compatible with LIGGGHTS/LAMMPS. Liquid bridges are created from surface liquid, capillary forces are applied, viscous forces are calculated, and surface liquid is transferred while bridges can rupture. Capillary interactions use the Soulie/Mikami approximation, with force depending on particle radius, surface tension, bridge volume, separation distance, and contact angle; the excerpt also gives a rupture-distance relation. Viscous coupling is represented by Stokes drag, FD = 6πμaΔU, where ΔU is the difference between particle and interpolated fluid velocity. In implementation terms, capillary forces are placed in the Hookean/contact model to reduce computation time, while viscous drag is implemented through the LAMMPS `fix viscous` command, with α = 6πa and an effective viscosity that may vary with invading-fluid saturation. The model requires parameters such as surface tension, initial surface-liquid content, and contact angle to vary or be defined according to saturation. Liquid transfer and bridge breakup are identified algorithmically, but this excerpt does not provide a detailed mass-conservation equation or transfer law. It also does not state the LIGGGHTS source-code status, identify Kumar (2021) or Schwarze (2013), or indicate that humidity is simulated.

"9", pages = "031002", month = "Aug", doi = "10.1088/2515-7639/ae9228", url = "https://doi.org/10.1088/2515-7639/ae9228", publisher = "IOP Publishing", issue = "3", issn = "2515-7639" } Abstract: Abstract To address the significant productivity challenges associated with the qualification and certification (Q&C) tasks of additively manufactured (AM) parts, which have traditionally relied on rigorous post‐build inspection and testing, we propose an integrated framework that combines model‐based qualification and certification (MBQ&C) with autonomous additive manufacturing (AAM). MBQ&C employs high‐fidelity predictive models, developed within the Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) paradigm, to simulate process–structure–property–performance relationships for assessing a part’s fitness for use. Since predictive models are commonly machine learning (ML)-based or reduced-order surrogates of validated physics models, they run efficiently, enabling timely inference. In parallel, the self-driving AAM utilises ML-based adaptive, closed‐loop control strategies to avoid, mitigate, or repair defects and anomalies during fabrication, thereby increasing the likelihood of producing acceptable parts. A key feature of the combined AAM-MBQ&C framework is that predictive models explicitly incorporate defects or anomalies that persist after the build, using instance-specific data captured via in-situ sensing. This customisation enables a build‐specific assessment of fitness for use, rather than relying on nominal or generic parameters. Such individualised evaluation provides a robust basis for Q&C-related acceptance decisions relating to each build. Additionally, the rapid solution capabilities of ML or reduced-order models enable the determination of a part’s suitability for service shortly after build completion. As the framework matures, it has the potential to substantially reduce reliance on conventional point‐design approaches—such as time‐consuming post‐build computed tomography scanning and costly destructive testing. Thus, the AAM-MBQ&C framework represents a transformative, scalable strategy for quality assurance of AM components, as parts produced within a stable, validated, and certified envelope can be certified with reduced testing. Key benefits include: (1) significant gains in Q&C productivity through efficient, model-centric assessment; (2) performance-based classification of defects into critical and non-critical categories; (3) the ability to predict potential deviations in the performance of parts affected by real-time, adaptive process control interventions relative to those produced under a certified process, and (4) the enabling of virtual Q&C for service environments that are difficult, hazardous, or impractical to access or reproduce experimentally. Collectively, these capabilities strengthen the business case for AM, particularly for high‐consequence and mission‐critical applications. Finally, although this work focuses on powder-based AM, the proposed techniques could be extended to AM processes employing alternative feedstock forms. Selected applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in metal additive manufacturing Valid Text Names: 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 1-2', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 2-3', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 3-3', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 3-4', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 4-5', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 5-8', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 8-9', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 9-12', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 12-14', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 14-15', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 15-17', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 17-19', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 19-20', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 20-21', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 21-22', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 22-23', 'rosen2026selectedapplicationsof pages 23-23' BibTex: @article{rosen2026selectedapplicationsof, author = "Rosen, David W. and Liu, Xiaofang", title = "Selected applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in metal additive manufacturing", year = "2026", journal = "Welding in the World", volume = "70", pages = "1299-1321", month = "Jan", doi = "10.1007/s40194-026-02335-z", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s40194-026-02335-z", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "4", issn = "0043-2288" } Abstract: Abstract Additive manufacturing (AM) represents a category of manufacturing processes that fabricates parts in a layer-by-layer manner. As such, AM provides unique advantages over conventional manufacturing processes such as the ability to fabricate highly complex geometries, to minimize material waste, and to enable mass customization, while having some limitations, such as high costs and complexities. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) enable these limitations to be addressed due to the data-rich environment in modern commercial AM machines with multiple sensors. However, its broader application across some AECOM sectors remains limited. A significant obstacle is that traditional DTs rely on deterministic models, which require deterministic input parameters. This limits their accuracy, as they do not account for the substantial uncertainties that are inherent in AECOM projects. These uncertainties are particularly pronounced in geotechnical design and construction. To address this challenge, we propose a probabilistic digital twin (PDT) framework that extends traditional DT methodologies by incorporating uncertainties and is tailored to the requirements of geotechnical design and construction. The PDT framework provides a structured approach to integrating all sources of uncertainty, including aleatoric, data, model, and prediction uncertainties, and propagates them throughout the entire modeling process. To ensure that site-specific conditions are accurately reflected as additional information is obtained, the PDT leverages Bayesian methods for model updating. The effectiveness of the PDT framework is showcased through an application to a highway foundation construction project, demonstrating its potential to integrate existing probabilistic methods to improve decision-making and project outcomes in the face of significant uncertainties. By embedding these methods within the PDT framework, we lower the barriers to practical implementation, making probabilistic approaches more accessible and applicable in real-world engineering workflows. Abstract:
Thermal energy storage technologies are essential for balancing energy demand and supply. There are three main types: sensible heat, latent heat, and thermochemical energy storage. Among them, thermochemical energy storage offers the highest energy density (1–3 GJ/m3) and long-term storage capability. Salt hydrates have attracted attention as energy storage materials due to their low cost, wide availability, and operating temperatures being well-suited for residential and low-temperature applications. This review focuses on the use of salt hydrates in sorption-based thermochemical energy storage systems. It summarizes the current state of knowledge, including screening studies of various salt hydrates, their thermodynamic and operational limitations, advantages, and performance in composite materials. This review also covers recent projects and common reactor designs used in TCES applications. Based on the literature analysis, the most promising salt hydrates for sorption-based TCES systems include SrCl2, SrBr2, K2CO3, MgSO4, MgCl2, and CaCl2. Despite the high theoretical energy density of many salt hydrates, future work should focus on experimental studies in large-scale reactor systems to better evaluate the practical discharge behavior of the energy storage system beyond theoretical hydration enthalpies or small-scale thermal analyses.

The excerpt discusses a custom LAMMPS-based implementation of capillary and viscous forces in a multiphase granular-flow model. It states that hydrodynamic forces are calculated using LAMMPS modules, noting that some modules are implemented while others lack complete or proper implementation. The proposed model adds liquid bridges from surface liquid, applies capillary forces, calculates viscous forces, and solves surface-liquid transfer and bridge breakup. Capillary interactions are computed within the Hookean model module to reduce computation time, whereas viscous forces are implemented as a LAMMPS fix because they do not involve particle-particle potentials. The capillary force model is based on Soulie’s formulation and a numerical approximation attributed to Mikami et al.; bridge rupture is also modeled. The excerpt further says that model constants should vary with saturation, including surface-liquid content and contact angle. It specifically mentions the LAMMPS `fix viscous` command, but it does not explicitly mention YADE, Yade CapillaryEngine, CapillaryPhys, liquid-meniscus interpolation, suction interpolation, or a LAMMPS GRANULAR capillary option. Thus, this passage supports characterization as a custom capillary/viscous implementation in LAMMPS, not a direct comparison with YADE engines or a named GRANULAR capillary feature.

This excerpt supports a cautious interpretation of Schwarze et al. (2013). For weakly wetted granular material, DEM reproduces qualitative features observed experimentally: shear-band structures remain similar to dry material, and adding small liquid quantities causes a substantial increase in apparent local shear viscosity, matching the experimental trend. However, the authors explicitly identify quantitative constitutive comparison as future work and note that simulations and experiments should be made more comparable, including use of the same gap width and improved understanding of local versus global viscosity. Thus, the excerpt does not establish close quantitative agreement in powder-scale shear rheology; it supports qualitative or trend-level agreement. The stated validation scope is also limited: the contact/liquid-bridge DEM model is checked against dry split-bottom ring-shear results and weakly wet two-particle collision data. The excerpt contains no information about Badetti (2018), MercuryDPM (2025), or LIGGGHTS (2013), so those works’ specific validation claims—particularly whether MercuryDPM validates two-sphere interactions rather than bulk powder rheology—cannot be assessed from this passage.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1140/epje/i2018-11677-8, doi:10.1140/epje/i2018-11677-8. This article has 61 citations.

Badetti et al. (2018) directly compare rheometric measurements with DEM simulations for wet spherical polystyrene beads in the pendular regime, where isolated liquid bridges form between grains. The experiments vary liquid content and apply controlled normal stress during steady, uniform, quasistatic shear; the simulations record comparable shear resistance and solid fraction as functions of reduced pressure P* = a²σ22/F0. The reported agreement is quantitative when the intergranular friction coefficient is calibrated from the dry material, specifically µ ≃ 0.09. The paper therefore supports a close measured–DEM correspondence for this controlled-moisture, bead-assembly setup, but not an exact match under every condition: the effective-stress assumption gives “very good (although not exact)” shear-strength predictions over the investigated range P* ≥ 0.5 and 0.05 ≤ µ ≤ 0.25. A pressure-independent Mohr–Coulomb cohesion is only a good approximation at sufficiently large P*, typically P* ≥ 2; cohesion can depend on P* more generally. This excerpt contains no information about Schwarze (2013), MercuryDPM (2025), or LIGGGHTS (2013), and thus cannot establish what those works specifically validate. In particular, it does not address two-sphere validation versus powder-rheology validation.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000038

From text 'gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 20-24'.

F. Gabrieli, P. Lambert, S. Cola, and F. Calvetti. Micromechanical modelling of erosion due to evaporation in a partially wet granular slope. International Journal for Numerical and Analytical Methods in Geomechanics, 36:918-943, May 2012. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/nag.1038, doi:10.1002/nag.1038. This article has 57 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt is relevant to the DEM evaporation-slope component of the question, but it contains no controlled-relative-humidity lactose, NaCl, or sucrose experiments and provides no validation of an FT4 test under controlled RH. The DEM study addressed computational cost by removing nearly motionless deep particles and replacing them with a fixed tilted boundary, reducing the model to 4,943 particles. It also accelerated evaporation using amplification factors of 10^5, 10^6, 10^8, and 10^9; the explicit integration critical timestep was 3×10^-6 s, making full laboratory-duration simulation impractical. The model reproduced the qualitative erosion mechanism seen experimentally: a dry front progressed into the slope, capillary bridges vanished, particles flowed along the surface, and neighboring particles detached. A later toe-collapse mechanism occurred as dried deeper strata pushed the slope laterally. Numerically, the simulated final profile had an upper angle of 35° and a toe angle of 21°, described as similar to experiment. Initial bridge volume was 3.8×10^-12 m^3; inferred initial suction ranged from approximately -200 to -2000 Pa and reached about -14,000 Pa near the surface during evaporation before vanishing when bridges broke. The authors cautioned that high amplification factors had not yet been fully verified against lower values such as 10^2, although the tested high factors produced no significant final-profile change.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'lu2017theeffectsof pages 3-7'.

Xiang-Yun Lu, Lan Chen, Chuan-Yu Wu, Hak-Kim Chan, and Tim Freeman. The effects of relative humidity on the flowability and dispersion performance of lactose mixtures. Materials, 10:592, May 2017. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma10060592, doi:10.3390/ma10060592. This article has 55 citations.

The excerpt reports controlled-humidity experiments on lactose blends using an FT4 powder rheometer and laser diffraction. Blends with different fine-lactose fractions were conditioned at four RH levels, evidently including 0%, 30%, 58%, and 85% RH, and assessed using dynamic flow metrics: normalized Basic Flow Energy (BFENorm), Specific Energy (SE, a shear-related measure), and Flow Rate Index (FRI). Both RH and fine-lactose fraction significantly influenced these properties, with the 20 wt.% fine fraction particularly sensitive. Flow energy fell rapidly at 85% RH because of moisture uptake, indicating poorer flow, while lactose flowability was relatively good at 30% and 58% RH. Dispersion was evaluated by Spraytec laser diffraction as fine particle fraction below 8.4 µm: 58% RH appeared beneficial, whereas 85% RH caused a dramatic FPF reduction, attributed to wet agglomerates and capillary forces. The excerpt provides no numerical FRI, SE, shear, or FPF values, no 48-hour conditioning detail, and no information about NaCl deliquescent relative humidity, sucrose bridge caking, DEM evaporation slopes, repose-angle tests, or comparison/validation between DEM and FT4 results. Thus, those topics cannot be reliably inferred from this excerpt.

From text 'gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 18-20'.

International Journal for Numerical and Analytical Methods in Geomechanics, 36:918-943, May 2012. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/nag.1038, doi:10.1002/nag.1038. This article has 57 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt is relevant to the DEM evaporation-slope and angle-of-repose portion of the question, but it contains no information about controlled-relative-humidity lactose experiments, NaCl deliquescence relative humidity (DRH), sucrose bridge caking, or FT4 validation. In the glass-sphere evaporation test, the initially wet slope had an angle of approximately 43°, compared with approximately 28° for dry material. As evaporation proceeded, the final profile became a two-angle talus: about 37° in the upper region and 19° at the toe. Particle-scale erosion occurred through detachment and rolling of small groups of particles, together with deeper-layer failures that pushed the toe laterally. Profile reconstruction showed deposition at roughly 18–22°, while the upper slope declined from 43° to 35–37°. The DEM represented evaporation by shrinking capillary-bridge volume according to the exposed air–liquid area and a depth-dependent exponential evaporation law. Calibration yielded rmax = 1.2 × 10^-8 m/s and c2 = 160 m^-1. The numerical slope used 11,628 balls, matched the experimental geometry, porosity, and density, and distributed the same water amount over contacts. After relaxation under gravity, the simulated initial slope angle equaled the real one; evaporation then tracked particle displacements, bridges, and contacts. The excerpt does not establish a direct FT4 comparison or validation.

The excerpt describes the DEM formulation used to model evaporation in a partially wet granular slope, rather than controlled-relative-humidity experiments on lactose, NaCl, or sucrose. Capillary attraction is strongest when particles are in contact and decreases as inter-particle distance increases. The capillary bridge ruptures when separation exceeds an empirical rupture distance that depends on liquid volume; after rupture, re-formation requires the grains to approach below that distance. To represent rough particle surfaces, the model imposes a minimum inter-particle distance of 10−5 m, which is particularly relevant as evaporation produces very small liquid volumes and rupture distances. The DEM implementation uses PFC3D, with linear elastic normal contact behavior and tangential elasticity plus plastic friction, while external routines apply the minimum-total-energy capillary-force approach. Potential bridges are assigned to particle pairs whose separation is below the rupture distance, and water is distributed iteratively among bridges under a specified water content. Reliable numerical details in this excerpt include particle radius R=1 mm, example bridge volume V=10−10 m3, contact angle 0°, and the assumed roughness/minimum gap smin=10−5 m. It gives no data on Lu lactose RH levels or FT4 flow/shear, NaCl DRH=75%, sucrose caking, or DEM repose-angle tests and their validation/comparison; therefore it cannot establish whether controlled-RH FT4 results were validated against DEM in the same study.

## pqac-00000043

From text 'samain2019characterizationofcaking pages 7-11'.

Sophie Samain, Mikel Leturia, Stéphane Mottelet, Mohammed Benali, and Khashayar Saleh. Characterization of caking for crystalline materials: comparison and statistical analysis of three mechanical tests. Chemical Engineering Science, 195:218-229, Feb 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2018.11.048, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2018.11.048. This article has 7 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a controlled-relative-humidity accelerated caking experiment for sucrose, not lactose, NaCl, DEM, or FT4 validation. A forced-convection device controlled temperature, RH, airflow, and normal stress; RH was adjustable from 5% to 93% at 25 °C, with a maximum flowrate of 15 NL/min. Sucrose crystals (315–400 µm) were humidified at 89.5% RH and 25 °C, explicitly above the deliquescence relative humidity, under 10 kPa normal stress and 15 NL/min airflow. Humidification lasted 40 minutes to 10 hours, producing water contents from 0.19% to 2.46%. Samples were then dried at 30% RH and 25 °C under the same stress and flow conditions, inducing drying and recrystallization; final water content was approximately 0.041% ± 0.01%. Caking was measured using uniaxial compression, diametrical compression, and shear tests. In the shear test, a defined fracture surface formed between two cells, and shear stress increased linearly until failure. For sucrose, maximum stress and energy generally increased with increasing water uptake before drying in the uniaxial and shear tests, while diametrical compression showed no significant response increase. The excerpt supplies no lactose RH series (0/30/58/85), NaCl DRH value, DEM evaporation-slope or repose-angle comparison, numerical model validation, or evidence that controlled-RH FT4 results were validated with DEM in the same study.

At 58% RH, dispersion was fairly good for all blends, suggesting an intermediate or optimal RH for powder flow and dry-powder-inhaler dispersion. At high humidity, liquid-bridge (capillary) forces were identified as the dominant adhesion mechanism. At 0% RH, electrostatic forces strongly affected fine particles, producing a parabolic rather than linear relationship between FPF and BFENorm; at 30%, 58%, and 85% RH, that relationship was linear. The conclusion states that dynamic-flow tests and permeability measurements identified fine-lactose fraction as the dominant factor affecting blend flowability. function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Humidity-aware DEM for an auger powder doser

**The modeling distinction is between liquid already present at contacts and water supplied as vapor.** Pendular-bridge DEM can predict the forces exerted by an assigned small liquid volume. It does not, by itself, determine whether humid air produces that volume, how quickly water reaches powder inside a reservoir, or whether a dissolved salt subsequently recrystallizes into a persistent bond. Those require a sorption/transport and, for salts, a phase-change model. A dry SJKR-cohesion model that reproduces salt’s mass per revolution is therefore a valuable baseline, but not evidence that its cohesion parameter represents moisture or will transfer across humidity histories. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032)

## Contact physics and humidity

In the **pendular regime**, isolated menisci connect particle pairs. A DEM contact law combines surface-tension and Laplace-pressure attraction, with force depending on separation, particle radii, surface tension, contact angle and bridge volume; the force persists after particles lose mechanical contact and vanishes at bridge rupture. A commonly used small-separation pull-off scale is approximately \(2\pi R_*\gamma\cos\theta\), where \(R_*\) is an effective radius; rupture distance scales approximately as \(V_b^{1/3}\), with contact-angle corrections. The simplified Willett approximation supplies a separation-dependent force; classical Willett is a more detailed fit. Lian gives a useful rupture-distance approximation. Rabinovich’s minimum-energy expression is another choice, but Gabrieli and colleagues note Lambert’s objection that adding a separate adhesion term to that energy-derived force can double-count it. These alternatives should be benchmarked with the same radius and volume conventions before interpreting fitted parameters physically. Isolated-pair laws cease to be sufficient when liquid bridges merge or liquid redistributes substantially. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000024)

**Relative humidity (RH) is not bridge volume.** For vapor-condensed water, the Kelvin relation links equilibrium meniscus curvature and capillary pressure to water activity, approximately \(p_c=-(RT/V_w)\ln(\mathrm{RH})\) when RH is expressed as a fraction, subject to curvature and sign conventions. One must additionally determine *which contacts contain water*, their accessible geometry and roughness, and their liquid volumes. At the micro-/millimetre scale, wet-granular simulations often prescribe bridge volume instead and calculate capillary pressure from it—an importantly different boundary condition. An empirical \(F_{\rm adh}(\mathrm{RH})\) or RH-dependent SJKR energy is a defensible **effective** model for rapid screening, but it cannot identify a unique liquid-bridge volume, sorption rate or salt phase from dosing data alone. Electrostatics may also change with RH, so an observed flow change need not be capillary-only. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000044)

For **NaCl**, the approximate deliquescence RH is **75%** for sufficiently large crystals under the conditions discussed by Hird and Bolton. Above deliquescence, a salt-solution film or bridge—not pure-water wetting of an inert sphere—can form; upon drying, dissolution and recrystallization can leave *solid bridges*. Thus the before/after-drying force can increase even when the final water content falls. Samain and colleagues demonstrated this sequence explicitly in a different crystalline material, sucrose: crystals were humidified at 89.5% RH, 25 °C, then dried at 30% RH; shear-measured cake strength increased with water taken up before drying. Their sucrose threshold, 85% RH, must **not** be assigned to NaCl or BaCl₂. I did not establish a reliable BaCl₂ deliquescence threshold or hydrate-transition conditions from the retrieved evidence; measure or obtain phase-specific data for the supplied BaCl₂ grade rather than borrowing NaCl’s threshold. Hygroscopic polymers, flour and metal powders likewise need separate sorption and surface-chemistry characterization. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000043)

To represent **exposure duration**, measure adsorption *and desorption* mass-versus-time curves at controlled temperature and RH, for both a thin sample and the actual filled reservoir. A practical reduced model uses an equilibrium sorption isotherm \(w_{\rm eq}(\mathrm{RH},T)\), an uptake law such as \(dw/dt=k[w_{\rm eq}-w]\), and, when needed, vapor diffusion through the bed or particle interiors. Map local \(w\) to bridge occupancy/volume and to independently evolving solid-bond fraction or strength. Treat adsorption, drying and repeated RH cycles separately; the first-order law is an approximation to test against measured kinetics, not a property supplied by a standard capillary contact law. DEM with shrinking bridge volumes has reproduced evaporation-driven granular-slope evolution, but that study prescribed an evaporation law and accelerated it heavily to make the mechanical simulation feasible—it did not solve arbitrary ambient-RH sorption in a doser. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

## Open-source implementations

The following comparison separates **documented wet-contact implementations** from an automatically coupled humid-air or salt-caking simulation.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

For your existing LIGGGHTS outlet model, adding a verified liquid-bridge contact law is a smaller change than changing simulators. Check the precise branch/version and wall-contact implementation; published LIGGGHTS Willett and wet-granulation implementations do not establish that your installation automatically transports vapor or creates bonds during idle exposure. MercuryDPM offers a documented alternative for comparing simplified/classical Willett and Bagheri pair laws; its published examples are **particle-pair** demonstrations. The retrieved LAMMPS evidence supports a *custom* granular contact implementation, not the claim that atomistic simulations with explicit water constitute an off-the-shelf auger-scale DEM humidity model. Yade’s commonly described `CapillaryEngine`/imposed-suction workflow should be checked against the intended version’s documentation: direct implementation documentation and controlled-RH validation were not independently recovered here. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000029)

## What has been validated?

- **Wet shear, with liquid deliberately added:** Badetti and colleagues obtained *quantitative* agreement between pendular-bridge DEM and rheometry of wet polystyrene beads after fixing interparticle friction from the dry material (approximately 0.09). Their controlled variable was added liquid content and applied stress, **not RH**. Their results also caution against treating bulk Mohr–Coulomb cohesion as a universal constant at low confining pressure. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000031)
- **LIGGGHTS bridge force and bulk rheology:** Schwarze and colleagues checked their Willett implementation against two-sphere separation experiments using 13.6, 31.3 and 74.2 nL bridges. Their wet-granular rheometer simulation reproduced *trends* in apparent viscosity, but the authors did not claim a completed quantitative constitutive match to the bulk experiment. This is pair-force and added-liquid validation, not a humid-air dosing test. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000030)
- **Repose/slope during drying:** Gabrieli and colleagues compared an evaporating wet-glass-bead slope with DEM: the experimental initial wet slope was about 43°, versus about 28° for dry material; the simulated final upper and toe angles were about **35° and 21°**, comparable with experimental upper and toe regions of about **37° and 19°**. This supports the *mechanism* of weakening as bridges evaporate, but its initial water was added and evaporation was prescribed, not inferred from controlled-RH exposure. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)
- **Controlled-RH powder flow, without matching DEM validation:** Lu and colleagues conditioned lactose blends for **48 h at 0%, 30%, 58% and 85% RH**, then measured FT4 dynamic-flow, permeability and shear responses. Flow was relatively good at intermediate RH and deteriorated at 85% RH; the change depended on fines fraction and was not simply monotonic. Their measured FT4 dynamic-property panels provide useful experimental comparators, **not** a validation of a humidity-aware DEM contact law. Sucrose humidity-cycle caking and shear-strength experiments likewise validate the importance of drying history, not an auger simulation. I did not find an equally substantiated *controlled-RH, same-powder* demonstration jointly matching DEM shear cell, repose and dosing/discharge across all conditions. (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000043)

## A tractable pre-/post-exposure dosing study

1. **Control and measure the material state.** Split each powder lot into dry/control, humid-exposed, and humid-then-redried aliquots. Log actual RH and temperature *inside or immediately at the reservoir*, exposure duration, initial fill/packing, sample mass gain or loss, and delay before each test. Include levels below and across NaCl’s approximate threshold, with suitable containment and material-specific limits; determine BaCl₂ transitions independently. Measure an uptake/desorption time course rather than assuming that the reservoir equilibrates in the same time as a thin test sample. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000043)
2. **Collect matched fingerprints and independent tests.** Randomize replicate runs across tilt, speed, fill level and tap setting; record the *distribution* of mass per revolution, tap-released mass, afterflow and zero-flow increments, including complete blockages. At the same conditioning state, measure the proposed ASTM D7891 FT4 and D6773 ring-shear responses, B213/B964 funnel flow or no-flow, B212/B527 bulk/tap densities, repose, B214/B822 size distributions, and loss on drying. Document sample preparation and consolidation: comparisons of FT4 and Schulze-family shear devices can differ systematically because pre-shearing differs. Hall/Carney no-flow is an informative outcome, not missing data. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000041)
3. **Calibrate hierarchically.** First constrain dry size distribution, packing, particle–particle and PLA/PETG-wall sliding/rolling friction, restitution and geometry with dry tests; use the supplied 105 mg/revolution salt match as an *out-of-sample baseline check* where possible. Then infer an effective humidity-dependent force, or explicit bridge occupancy/volume and rupture law if independently measured sorption supports them. Add persistent solid bonds for humid-then-dried salt only if that history requires them. Fit a joint likelihood for continuous mass and time outputs, tap response, and binomial/sequence-aware no-flow events; include balance noise, run-to-run packing and simulator discrepancy. Repose alone cannot separate friction, rolling resistance and adhesion: published calibration examples produce different parameter sets across slump and hopper tests. Report posterior *effective parameters and correlations*, not an unjustified unique microscopic surface energy. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000040)
4. **Spend DEM runs on discrimination, not brute-force posterior sampling.** At the stated **26–30 CPU-min per simulated revolution**, screen sensitivity and fit an uncertainty-aware surrogate using selected tilt/speed/RH-history conditions, then run direct DEM checks at posterior extremes and held-out conditions. Advance the sorption/solid-bond state on the measured exposure-time scale and use DEM for the comparatively short dispensing/tapping intervals; explicitly model the 3 mm outlet and particle–printed-wall interactions. A repeatable failure of a liquid-only model to predict the redried sample’s no-flow rate or tap response would be evidence to test a caking/bond-history model, **not** proof of a particular salt bridge chemistry. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000032)
5. **Test transfer to additive-manufacturing spreading separately.** Carry the *posterior distribution* of contact and size parameters into a recoater/roller geometry and measure deposited-layer mass or density, coverage/voids and surface roughness at controlled RH and spreading speed. Dosing from an auger, gravity funnel flow and formation of a thin moving powder bed impose different stresses and boundaries; even a well-matched dosing fingerprint does not alone validate spreadability. Published spreading work assesses layer packing and nonuniformity directly rather than identifying layer quality from repose alone. (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036)

**Bottom line:** A before/after humid-air dosing experiment is feasible now as an experimentally conditioned, state-dependent DEM comparison. Predicting its *time course* or irreversible salt caking requires measured sorption/phase history and new coupling; none of the wet-bridge implementations established here should be treated as a ready-made, validated RH-to-NaCl/BaCl₂-cake-to-auger-to-powder-bed pipeline. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000041)"}

Those require a sorption/transport and, for salts, a phase-change model. A dry SJKR-cohesion model that reproduces salt’s mass per revolution is therefore a valuable baseline, but not evidence that its cohesion parameter represents moisture or will transfer across humidity histories. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032)

## Contact physics and humidity

In the **pendular regime**, isolated menisci connect particle pairs. A DEM contact law combines surface-tension and Laplace-pressure attraction, with force depending on separation, particle radii, surface tension, contact angle and bridge volume; the force persists after particles lose mechanical contact and vanishes at bridge rupture. A commonly used small-separation pull-off scale is approximately \(2\pi R_*\gamma\cos\theta\), where \(R_*\) is an effective radius; rupture distance scales approximately as \(V_b^{1/3}\), with contact-angle corrections. The simplified Willett approximation supplies a separation-dependent force; classical Willett is a more detailed fit. Lian gives a useful rupture-distance approximation. Rabinovich’s minimum-energy expression is another choice, but Gabrieli and colleagues note Lambert’s objection that adding a separate adhesion term to that energy-derived force can double-count it. These alternatives should be benchmarked with the same radius and volume conventions before interpreting fitted parameters physically. Isolated-pair laws cease to be sufficient when liquid bridges merge or liquid redistributes substantially. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000024)

**Relative humidity (RH) is not bridge volume.** For vapor-condensed water, the Kelvin relation links equilibrium meniscus curvature and capillary pressure to water activity, approximately \(p_c=-(RT/V_w)\ln(\mathrm{RH})\) when RH is expressed as a fraction, subject to curvature and sign conventions. One must additionally determine *which contacts contain water*, their accessible geometry and roughness, and their liquid volumes. At the micro-/millimetre scale, wet-granular simulations often prescribe bridge volume instead and calculate capillary pressure from it—an importantly different boundary condition. An empirical \(F_{\rm adh}(\mathrm{RH})\) or RH-dependent SJKR energy is a defensible **effective** model for rapid screening, but it cannot identify a unique liquid-bridge volume, sorption rate or salt phase from dosing data alone. Electrostatics may also change with RH, so an observed flow change need not be capillary-only. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000044)

For **NaCl**, the approximate deliquescence RH is **75%** for sufficiently large crystals under the conditions discussed by Hird and Bolton. Above deliquescence, a salt-solution film or bridge—not pure-water wetting of an inert sphere—can form; upon drying, dissolution and recrystallization can leave *solid bridges*. Thus the before/after-drying force can increase even when the final water content falls. Samain and colleagues demonstrated this sequence explicitly in a different crystalline material, sucrose: crystals were humidified at 89.5% RH, 25 °C, then dried at 30% RH; shear-measured cake strength increased with water taken up before drying. Their sucrose threshold, 85% RH, must **not** be assigned to NaCl or BaCl₂. I did not establish a reliable BaCl₂ deliquescence threshold or hydrate-transition conditions from the retrieved evidence; measure or obtain phase-specific data for the supplied BaCl₂ grade rather than borrowing NaCl’s threshold. Hygroscopic polymers, flour and metal powders likewise need separate sorption and surface-chemistry characterization. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000043)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

- **Wet shear, with liquid deliberately added:** Badetti and colleagues obtained *quantitative* agreement between pendular-bridge DEM and rheometry of wet polystyrene beads after fixing interparticle friction from the dry material (approximately 0.09). - **LIGGGHTS bridge force and bulk rheology:** Schwarze and colleagues checked their Willett implementation against two-sphere separation experiments using 13.6, 31.3 and 74.2 nL bridges. Sucrose humidity-cycle caking and shear-strength experiments likewise validate the importance of drying history, not an auger simulation. Measure an uptake/desorption time course rather than assuming that the reservoir equilibrates in the same time as a thin test sample. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000043)

Hall/Carney no-flow is an informative outcome, not missing data. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000041)

Add persistent solid bonds for humid-then-dried salt only if that history requires them. state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How do physics-based simulations represent humidity and moisture effects on fine-powder flow: liquid (capillary) bridge force models in DEM (Willett, Rabinovich, Lian, pendular regime), relative-humidity-dependent cohesion, hygroscopic salts such as NaCl and BaCl2 with deliquescence and caking by solid bridges, and moisture sorption kinetics? Which open-source DEM codes implement capillary forces (LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, Yade, MercuryDPM)? How have these models been validated against shear-cell, angle-of-repose or flow-rate measurements at controlled humidity, and could they model an experiment in which a powder is dosed before and after exposure to humid air?
