# Humidity-aware DEM for an auger powder doser

**The modeling distinction is between liquid already present at contacts and water supplied as vapor.** Pendular-bridge DEM can predict the forces exerted by an assigned small liquid volume. It does not, by itself, determine whether humid air produces that volume, how quickly water reaches powder inside a reservoir, or whether a dissolved salt subsequently recrystallizes into a persistent bond. Those require a sorption/transport and, for salts, a phase-change model. A dry SJKR-cohesion model that reproduces salt’s mass per revolution is therefore a valuable baseline, but not evidence that its cohesion parameter represents moisture or will transfer across humidity histories. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032)

## Contact physics and humidity

In the **pendular regime**, isolated menisci connect particle pairs. A DEM contact law combines surface-tension and Laplace-pressure attraction, with force depending on separation, particle radii, surface tension, contact angle and bridge volume; the force persists after particles lose mechanical contact and vanishes at bridge rupture. A commonly used small-separation pull-off scale is approximately \(2\pi R_*\gamma\cos\theta\), where \(R_*\) is an effective radius; rupture distance scales approximately as \(V_b^{1/3}\), with contact-angle corrections. The simplified Willett approximation supplies a separation-dependent force; classical Willett is a more detailed fit. Lian gives a useful rupture-distance approximation. Rabinovich’s minimum-energy expression is another choice, but Gabrieli and colleagues note Lambert’s objection that adding a separate adhesion term to that energy-derived force can double-count it. These alternatives should be benchmarked with the same radius and volume conventions before interpreting fitted parameters physically. Isolated-pair laws cease to be sufficient when liquid bridges merge or liquid redistributes substantially. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000024)

**Relative humidity (RH) is not bridge volume.** For vapor-condensed water, the Kelvin relation links equilibrium meniscus curvature and capillary pressure to water activity, approximately \(p_c=-(RT/V_w)\ln(\mathrm{RH})\) when RH is expressed as a fraction, subject to curvature and sign conventions. One must additionally determine *which contacts contain water*, their accessible geometry and roughness, and their liquid volumes. At the micro-/millimetre scale, wet-granular simulations often prescribe bridge volume instead and calculate capillary pressure from it—an importantly different boundary condition. An empirical \(F_{\rm adh}(\mathrm{RH})\) or RH-dependent SJKR energy is a defensible **effective** model for rapid screening, but it cannot identify a unique liquid-bridge volume, sorption rate or salt phase from dosing data alone. Electrostatics may also change with RH, so an observed flow change need not be capillary-only. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000044)

For **NaCl**, the approximate deliquescence RH is **75%** for sufficiently large crystals under the conditions discussed by Hird and Bolton. Above deliquescence, a salt-solution film or bridge—not pure-water wetting of an inert sphere—can form; upon drying, dissolution and recrystallization can leave *solid bridges*. Thus the before/after-drying force can increase even when the final water content falls. Samain and colleagues demonstrated this sequence explicitly in a different crystalline material, sucrose: crystals were humidified at 89.5% RH, 25 °C, then dried at 30% RH; shear-measured cake strength increased with water taken up before drying. Their sucrose threshold, 85% RH, must **not** be assigned to NaCl or BaCl₂. I did not establish a reliable BaCl₂ deliquescence threshold or hydrate-transition conditions from the retrieved evidence; measure or obtain phase-specific data for the supplied BaCl₂ grade rather than borrowing NaCl’s threshold. Hygroscopic polymers, flour and metal powders likewise need separate sorption and surface-chemistry characterization. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000043)

To represent **exposure duration**, measure adsorption *and desorption* mass-versus-time curves at controlled temperature and RH, for both a thin sample and the actual filled reservoir. A practical reduced model uses an equilibrium sorption isotherm \(w_{\rm eq}(\mathrm{RH},T)\), an uptake law such as \(dw/dt=k[w_{\rm eq}-w]\), and, when needed, vapor diffusion through the bed or particle interiors. Map local \(w\) to bridge occupancy/volume and to independently evolving solid-bond fraction or strength. Treat adsorption, drying and repeated RH cycles separately; the first-order law is an approximation to test against measured kinetics, not a property supplied by a standard capillary contact law. DEM with shrinking bridge volumes has reproduced evaporation-driven granular-slope evolution, but that study prescribed an evaporation law and accelerated it heavily to make the mechanical simulation feasible—it did not solve arbitrary ambient-RH sorption in a doser. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

## Open-source implementations

The following comparison separates **documented wet-contact implementations** from an automatically coupled humid-air or salt-caking simulation.

| Code | Documented capillary-force implementation | Humidity / kinetic support | Validation caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LIGGGHTS** | Custom Willett liquid-bridge model published for v2.3.2; a separate wet-granulation implementation used Mikami forces with surface-liquid redistribution and finite-rate transfer. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027) | Prescribed bridge volumes or tracked surface liquid; the cited implementations do **not** demonstrate a built-in ambient-RH, sorption, deliquescence, or solid-bridge model. | Willett force law was checked against two-sphere experiments; bulk wet-rheology agreement was mainly qualitative rather than a controlled-RH validation. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000030) |
| **LAMMPS** | A custom granular implementation placed Soulie/Mikami capillary forces in a Hookean contact model and used `fix viscous` separately. Atomistic LAMMPS simulations with explicit water are a different scale and are not evidence of a native general-purpose granular capillary law. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029) | Humidity-to-bridge formation, sorption kinetics, salt deliquescence, and caking require user coupling or custom code in the retrieved evidence. | The retrieved implementation is custom, not a documented standard granular-capillary feature; no controlled-RH bulk-flow validation was established. |
| **Yade** | `CapillaryEngine` for pendular menisci under imposed suction is widely referenced, but this capability was **not independently verified in the retrieved source set**; check the exact Yade version, build options, examples, and documentation before selection. | Do not equate imposed suction with a solved RH/sorption field; salt deliquescence, moisture transport, evaporation, and solid-bridge formation would still require additional models. | No retrieved evidence supports claiming controlled-RH powder-flow or hygroscopic-salt validation for this implementation. |
| **MercuryDPM** | Existing simplified `LiquidBridgeWillet`; published 2025 additions `LiquidBridgeClassicalWillet` and `LiquidBridgeBagheri`, including an unequal-particle extension of Bagheri. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016) | Bridge volume, contact angle, surface tension, separation, formation after contact, and rupture are represented; Bagheri also returns bridge area useful for a future evaporation model. No RH/sorption or salt-phase-transition solver was demonstrated. | Publication demonstrates particle-pair force behavior for 10 and 80 nL bridges, not controlled-humidity shear-cell, repose, discharge, or dosing validation. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000016) |


*Table: Comparison of documented wet-contact capabilities in four open-source particle codes. It separates implemented liquid-bridge laws from ambient-humidity, sorption, deliquescence, and bulk-flow capabilities that would require additional modeling or verification.*

For your existing LIGGGHTS outlet model, adding a verified liquid-bridge contact law is a smaller change than changing simulators. Check the precise branch/version and wall-contact implementation; published LIGGGHTS Willett and wet-granulation implementations do not establish that your installation automatically transports vapor or creates bonds during idle exposure. MercuryDPM offers a documented alternative for comparing simplified/classical Willett and Bagheri pair laws; its published examples are **particle-pair** demonstrations. The retrieved LAMMPS evidence supports a *custom* granular contact implementation, not the claim that atomistic simulations with explicit water constitute an off-the-shelf auger-scale DEM humidity model. Yade’s commonly described `CapillaryEngine`/imposed-suction workflow should be checked against the intended version’s documentation: direct implementation documentation and controlled-RH validation were not independently recovered here. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000029)

Their controlled variable was added liquid content and applied stress, **not RH**. Their results also caution against treating bulk Mohr–Coulomb cohesion as a universal constant at low confining pressure. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000031)

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general guidance for calibrating cohesive-material DEM models but does not document the requested Willett, Rabinovich, or Lian capillary-bridge force laws, rupture distances, Kelvin relative-humidity condensation equations or limitations, salt-deliquescence caking and sorption kinetics, or validated implementations in LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, Yade, or MercuryDPM. Its relevant methodological points are that cohesive calibration requires accounting for the coupled influence of cohesion and non-cohesive parameters, and therefore generally needs more simulation runs than non-cohesive calibration. Experiments should be selected for sensitivity to the parameters being calibrated; an angle-of-repose test is only useful for cohesion if changes in cohesion or moisture produce statistically distinguishable responses. A single bulk experiment may not uniquely determine multiple parameters, so combining experiments is recommended. Optimization can calibrate many inputs, but it cannot compensate for insensitive physical experiments or insensitive numerical models. The paper’s stated scope mainly concerns mining and, to some degree, agriculture, rather than pharmaceutical and food powders.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a discrete-element modelling study of evaporation-induced erosion in a partially wet granular slope. At the particle scale, a minimum-energy capillary-bridge approach was used to model both relaxation of two spherical particles and bridge evaporation; the evaporation rate was reported to influence whether bridge failure occurred quasi-statically or dynamically. Triaxial simulations examined different water contents and confining pressures, finding that capillary-related strength enhancement was more pronounced in shallow soils under low confining stress and relatively high saturation, even in the pendular regime. A small-scale slope evaporation test was also simulated with shrinking capillary-bridge volumes. The erosion process was divided into equilibrated deep material, a dry shallow layer tending toward the material angle of repose, and a transitional middle layer more susceptible to erosion. Two displacement phases were identified: shallow particle erosion and deposition at the toe, followed by formation of a deeper slide surface and rigid movement of much of the slope. However, this excerpt does not provide a humidity-dependent Kelvin equation, relative-humidity-controlled evaporation or diffusion kinetics, nor an explicit distinction between RH exposure and pre-added liquid. It also gives no exact numerical comparison or measured numerical agreement for angle of repose, avalanche, or discharge experiments; it only mentions qualitative repose-angle and erosion observations.

contexts.context: The study identifies five particle-bond types: interparticle forces, mobile/immobile liquid bridges, solid bridges, and entanglement; solid bridges are strongest and irreversible. For deliquescent crystals, humidity above the material-specific DRH creates aqueous liquid bridges; lowering RH causes efflorescence and recrystallized solid bridges, producing hard cakes. Sucrose has DRH 85% at 25°C. Bridge strength depends on RH, temperature, stress, solubility, particle shape, and size. An accelerated, controlled caking device produced homogeneous samples within hours. Comparing compression, tensile, and shear tests, shear was most sensitive and repeatable, with cake strength linearly related to water uptake.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. contexts.context: The excerpt describes DEM simulations of partly wet granular materials in a split-bottom ring-shear rheometer. Explicit capillary forces are added to particle contacts; Grima and Wypych instead use an implicit capillary model. Experiments used F35 sand (ρ≈1400 kg/m³, fill height ≈70 mm), liquid contents of 1–2%, and external pressures of 4–8 kPa, exceeding hydrostatic pressure (~1 kPa). Wet materials showed markedly higher apparent viscosity than dry sand above 10 s⁻¹ and shear-thinning behavior fitted by \(η_g=K|\dotγ_g|^{-α}\), with binder-dependent \(K,α\).

contexts.context: Capillary bridges from adsorbed water can form even at low RH and dominate adhesion, depending on bridge geometry, contact angle, surface tension, and roughness. Established models often assume circular, axisymmetric menisci with negligible gravity; errors are under 5% for some angles but increase near vapor saturation. Roughness generally reduces measured pull-off force by limiting contact points, despite simplified theories predicting otherwise. Surface heterogeneity, line tension, microscopic contact angle, and deformation are often neglected. The study uses LAMMPS to simulate liquid bridges between silicon surfaces and compares geometries, roughness, theory, and AFM experiments.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes LIGGGHTS soft-sphere DEM with spring–dashpot–slider contact forces and an added liquid-bridge model. It explicitly tracks “liquid-bridge formation, rupture,” and bridge effects on interparticle forces, with liquid redistributed by particle collisions and screw-driven convection. Models can include wetting behavior, capillary/viscous bridge formation, binder dissolution, and parameters such as liquid-to-solid ratio, viscosity, and pore saturation. However, uniform liquid distribution is identified as unrealistic experimentally, and particle breakage/attrition may be omitted. No controlled-humidity, deliquescence, sorption-kinetics, or validation results are provided.

contexts.context: Bagheri, Roy, and Pöschel (2024) implement capillary liquid-bridge forces in the open-source MercuryDPM DEM code. MercuryDPM previously had a simplified Willett model; new models are “LiquidBridgeClassicalWillet” and “LiquidBridgeBagheri,” with Bagheri extended to unequal particle sizes and providing bridge surface area relevant to evaporation. Bridges form on contact, exert force versus separation, and rupture at a critical distance. The study uses two-particle collision tests (0.5/0.8 mm and 0.5/1 mm particles), with \(E=5\) MPa, \(\nu=0.35\), \(\rho=2000\) kg/m³, \(\gamma=0.079\) N/m, contact angle \(0^\circ\), and 10/80 nL bridges.

contexts.context: The excerpt validates a DEM capillary-bridge model against Willett’s two-particle separation experiments: radius 2.4 mm, surface tension 20.6 mN/m, complete wetting (θ=0°), and bridge volumes 13.6, 31.3, and 74.2 nL. Further wet-granular simulations vary contact angle 0–20° and use 4.2 or 42 nL bridges, corresponding to approximately 0.15% or 1.5% liquid/dry mass. Simulations reproduce dry-material shear stress and shear-band behavior, then assess liquid bridges’ effect on apparent viscosity. Runs last 20 s, averaging 15–20 s; long-term relaxation is not resolved. No humidity, deliquescence, sorption kinetics, code comparisons, or dosing validation is described.

contexts.context: In lactose blends, fine-particle content and RH strongly affected flow. Flow energy rapidly decreased at 85% RH because of moisture uptake; 20 wt.% fines were most sensitive. Above 65% RH, capillary/liquid-bridge and van der Waals forces dominated, whereas below 65% van der Waals and electrostatic forces prevailed. At 85% RH, wet agglomerates formed and dispersion/FPF (particles <8.4 µm) dropped dramatically; 58% RH sometimes improved dispersion. Permeability also changed with fines and RH. Measurements used FT4 flow energy/permeability, laser diffraction at 60 L/min, and ANOVA (α=0.05), but no DEM implementation or validation was reported.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes DEM-ready capillary-force formulations for liquid bridges between particles. Simplified Soulié/Richefeu modeling gives \(F_{cap}=-2\pi R\gamma\cos\theta\,e^{-s/\lambda}\), while Rabinovich/Lambert energy-based expressions depend on separation \(s\), bridge volume \(V\), radius \(R\), surface tension \(\gamma\), and contact angle \(\theta\). For example, Lambert’s equation is \(F_{cap}=-2\pi R\gamma\cos\theta/[1+s/(2d)]\). contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How do physics-based simulations represent humidity and moisture effects on fine-powder flow: liquid (capillary) bridge force models in DEM (Willett, Rabinovich, Lian, pendular regime), relative-humidity-dependent cohesion, hygroscopic salts such as NaCl and BaCl2 with deliquescence and caking by solid bridges, and moisture sorption kinetics? Which open-source DEM codes implement capillary forces (LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, Yade, MercuryDPM)? How have these models been validated against shear-cell, angle-of-repose or flow-rate measurements at controlled humidity, and could they model an experiment in which a powder is dosed before and after exposure to humid air?

(2021) describe a particle-scale wet capillary-bridge implementation in which cohesive forces are calculated with the Mikami et al. capillary-force model, while liquid distribution during bridge formation is tracked using model C of Mohan et al. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a wet-particle implementation conceptually compatible with LIGGGHTS/LAMMPS. Liquid bridges are created from surface liquid, capillary forces are applied, viscous forces are calculated, and surface liquid is transferred while bridges can rupture. contexts.context: This excerpt supports a cautious interpretation of Schwarze et al. (2013). For weakly wetted granular material, DEM reproduces qualitative features observed experimentally: shear-band structures remain similar to dry material, and adding small liquid quantities causes a substantial increase in apparent local shear viscosity, matching the experimental trend. However, the authors explicitly identify quantitative constitutive comparison as future work and note that simulations and experiments should be made more comparable, including use of the same gap width and improved understanding of local versus global viscosity. Thus, the excerpt does not establish close quantitative agreement in powder-scale shear rheology; it supports qualitative or trend-level agreement. contexts.context: Badetti et al. (2018) directly compare rheometric measurements with DEM simulations for wet spherical polystyrene beads in the pendular regime, where isolated liquid bridges form between grains. The experiments vary liquid content and apply controlled normal stress during steady, uniform, quasistatic shear; the simulations record comparable shear resistance and solid fraction as functions of reduced pressure P* = a²σ22/F0. The reported agreement is quantitative when the intergranular friction coefficient is calibrated from the dry material, specifically µ ≃ 0.09. The paper therefore supports a close measured–DEM correspondence for this controlled-moisture, bead-assembly setup, but not an exact match under every condition: the effective-stress assumption gives “very good (although not exact)” shear-strength predictions over the investigated range P* ≥ 0.5 and 0.05 ≤ µ ≤ 0.25. A pressure-independent Mohr–Coulomb cohesion is only a good approximation at sufficiently large P*, typically P* ≥ 2; cohesion can depend on P* more generally. This excerpt contains no information about Schwarze (2013), MercuryDPM (2025), or LIGGGHTS (2013), and thus cannot establish what those works specifically validate. contexts.context: The excerpt provides published evidence that angle of repose alone does not uniquely identify DEM interparticle parameters. In the dry-material calibration, particle-particle sliding friction was the same in the slump and hopper-discharge tests, but the hopper test required a lower rolling-friction value. The authors therefore could not identify one parameter set that accurately reproduced both tests, demonstrating calibration non-uniqueness even before cohesion was introduced. For moist cohesive material, the pile became irregular, making repose angle difficult to define. Moreover, cohesion energy density had little effect on the repose angle formed after hopper discharge, while it significantly affected the shear angle of the material remaining in the hopper. Consequently, the shear angle—not repose alone—was used to calibrate cohesion in that test. Cohesion values calibrated from the slump and hopper tests differed significantly, further indicating test- and response-dependent parameter identifiability. The excerpt also notes that spherical particles can produce undesirable flow behaviour and that rolling-resistance model choice can cause creep, relevant limitations when interpreting calibration results. However, this excerpt contains no evidence concerning FT4 versus Schulze pre-shear differences, nor does it discuss predicting additive-manufacturing powder-bed spreading using deposited-layer density, coverage, or roughness. Those topics require additional sources from the cited literature or other published studies.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general support for limitations in calibrating DEM powder-spreading models, but it does not identify the specific published studies requested. It states that cohesive energy density is among the most influential DEM parameters and that omitting cohesion overestimates powder mobility, indicating that calibration based on a single bulk flowability measure may be insufficient. It also emphasizes that conventional flowability tests do not reproduce LPBF’s constrained, dynamic deposition geometry; therefore, metrics such as angle of repose should be treated as indicators rather than unique predictors of spreading behavior. The passage does not discuss whether repose angle uniquely determines sliding friction, rolling resistance, or adhesion, and it contains no evidence comparing FT4 and Schulze measurements or their differing pre-shear conditions. Nor does it provide specific studies establishing the scope or accuracy of predicting additive-manufacturing powder-bed spreading using deposited-layer density, coverage, or roughness. The closest relevant implication is that process-specific experiments and DEM simulations should be combined, with powder-bed formation and packing density treated as performance-relevant outcomes. Exact sources for the FT4-versus-Schulze comparison and deposited-layer validation must therefore be retrieved from the article’s cited literature or other publications.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides evidence that repose-angle-type measurements are useful for assessing powder spreadability but do not by themselves fully characterize powder-bed quality or all DEM contact parameters. Dynamic angle of repose (AOR) is associated with spreadability: smaller values indicate better spreading, while increasing rake velocity raises the dynamic AOR and its rate of variation. The resulting high-velocity beds show reduced packing density and poorer surface quality, including unfilled and non-uniform regions. The excerpt also identifies particle segregation during raking, with coarse particles accumulating at the moving pile front; this can produce spatially varying packing density and increase defect risk. More broadly, the reported relationship between packing density and coordination number is sensitive to particle type, size, and adhesion conditions, indicating that calibration or interpretation cannot rely on a single scalar metric. However, this passage does not mention FT4 or Schulze shear testing, pre-shear conditions, or explicitly demonstrate that identical repose angles can correspond to different sliding resistance, rolling resistance, and adhesion parameters. It also does not provide a formal validation scope for DEM predictions using deposited-layer density, coverage, and roughness beyond the reported rake-velocity comparisons.

contexts.context: This excerpt is relevant to the DEM evaporation-slope component of the question, but it contains no controlled-relative-humidity lactose, NaCl, or sucrose experiments and provides no validation of an FT4 test under controlled RH. The DEM study addressed computational cost by removing nearly motionless deep particles and replacing them with a fixed tilted boundary, reducing the model to 4,943 particles. It also accelerated evaporation using amplification factors of 10^5, 10^6, 10^8, and 10^9; the explicit integration critical timestep was 3×10^-6 s, making full laboratory-duration simulation impractical. The model reproduced the qualitative erosion mechanism seen experimentally: a dry front progressed into the slope, capillary bridges vanished, particles flowed along the surface, and neighboring particles detached. A later toe-collapse mechanism occurred as dried deeper strata pushed the slope laterally. Numerically, the simulated final profile had an upper angle of 35° and a toe angle of 21°, described as similar to experiment. Initial bridge volume was 3.8×10^-12 m^3; inferred initial suction ranged from approximately -200 to -2000 Pa and reached about -14,000 Pa near the surface during evaporation before vanishing when bridges broke. The authors cautioned that high amplification factors had not yet been fully verified against lower values such as 10^2, although the tested high factors produced no significant final-profile change.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the DEM formulation used to model evaporation in a partially wet granular slope, rather than controlled-relative-humidity experiments on lactose, NaCl, or sucrose. Capillary attraction is strongest when particles are in contact and decreases as inter-particle distance increases. The capillary bridge ruptures when separation exceeds an empirical rupture distance that depends on liquid volume; after rupture, re-formation requires the grains to approach below that distance. To represent rough particle surfaces, the model imposes a minimum inter-particle distance of 10−5 m, which is particularly relevant as evaporation produces very small liquid volumes and rupture distances. The DEM implementation uses PFC3D, with linear elastic normal contact behavior and tangential elasticity plus plastic friction, while external routines apply the minimum-total-energy capillary-force approach. Potential bridges are assigned to particle pairs whose separation is below the rupture distance, and water is distributed iteratively among bridges under a specified water content. Reliable numerical details in this excerpt include particle radius R=1 mm, example bridge volume V=10−10 m3, contact angle 0°, and the assumed roughness/minimum gap smin=10−5 m. It gives no data on Lu lactose RH levels or FT4 flow/shear, NaCl DRH=75%, sucrose caking, or DEM repose-angle tests and their validation/comparison; therefore it cannot establish whether controlled-RH FT4 results were validated against DEM in the same study.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports controlled-humidity experiments on lactose blends using an FT4 powder rheometer and laser diffraction. Blends with different fine-lactose fractions were conditioned at four RH levels, evidently including 0%, 30%, 58%, and 85% RH, and assessed using dynamic flow metrics: normalized Basic Flow Energy (BFENorm), Specific Energy (SE, a shear-related measure), and Flow Rate Index (FRI). Both RH and fine-lactose fraction significantly influenced these properties, with the 20 wt.% fine fraction particularly sensitive. Flow energy fell rapidly at 85% RH because of moisture uptake, indicating poorer flow, while lactose flowability was relatively good at 30% and 58% RH. Dispersion was evaluated by Spraytec laser diffraction as fine particle fraction below 8.4 µm: 58% RH appeared beneficial, whereas 85% RH caused a dramatic FPF reduction, attributed to wet agglomerates and capillary forces. The excerpt provides no numerical FRI, SE, shear, or FPF values, no 48-hour conditioning detail, and no information about NaCl deliquescent relative humidity, sucrose bridge caking, DEM evaporation slopes, repose-angle tests, or comparison/validation between DEM and FT4 results. contexts.context: This excerpt is relevant to the DEM evaporation-slope and angle-of-repose portion of the question, but it contains no information about controlled-relative-humidity lactose experiments, NaCl deliquescence relative humidity (DRH), sucrose bridge caking, or FT4 validation. In the glass-sphere evaporation test, the initially wet slope had an angle of approximately 43°, compared with approximately 28° for dry material. As evaporation proceeded, the final profile became a two-angle talus: about 37° in the upper region and 19° at the toe. Particle-scale erosion occurred through detachment and rolling of small groups of particles, together with deeper-layer failures that pushed the toe laterally. Profile reconstruction showed deposition at roughly 18–22°, while the upper slope declined from 43° to 35–37°. The DEM represented evaporation by shrinking capillary-bridge volume according to the exposed air–liquid area and a depth-dependent exponential evaporation law. Calibration yielded rmax = 1.2 × 10^-8 m/s and c2 = 160 m^-1. The numerical slope used 11,628 balls, matched the experimental geometry, porosity, and density, and distributed the same water amount over contacts. After relaxation under gravity, the simulated initial slope angle equaled the real one; evaporation then tracked particle displacements, bridges, and contacts. The excerpt does not establish a direct FT4 comparison or validation.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative findings from Lu et al.’s controlled-relative-humidity lactose experiments. Lactose powder flowability was relatively good at 30% and 58% RH, whereas the 5, 10, and 20 wt.% fine-lactose blends had their poorest flowability and dispersion performance after conditioning at 85% RH. The 20 wt.% blend was reportedly less sensitive to humidity in terms of flowability. At 58% RH, dispersion was fairly good for all blends, suggesting an intermediate or optimal RH for powder flow and dry-powder-inhaler dispersion. At high humidity, liquid-bridge (capillary) forces were identified as the dominant adhesion mechanism. At 0% RH, electrostatic forces strongly affected fine particles, producing a parabolic rather than linear relationship between FPF and BFENorm; at 30%, 58%, and 85% RH, that relationship was linear. The conclusion states that dynamic-flow tests and permeability measurements identified fine-lactose fraction as the dominant factor affecting blend flowability. This excerpt does not provide numerical flow-rate-index or shear values, does not state a 48-hour conditioning duration, and contains no NaCl deliquescent-relative-humidity, sucrose-caking, evaporation-slope DEM, repose-test, or DEM-validation results. It therefore cannot substantiate a comparison between controlled-RH FT4 measurements and DEM within the same study.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns controlled caking experiments on sucrose rather than lactose, sodium chloride, or DEM-based flow modeling. Sucrose is described as a deliquescent crystalline powder with a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of 85% at 25 °C. Partial deliquescence creates aqueous liquid bridges between crystals; reducing RH below the DRH causes efflorescence and recrystallization into solid bridges, producing a hard cake. The study developed an accelerated device to produce homogeneous sucrose cakes under controlled humidity, temperature, and stress in a few hours. It compared uniaxial compression, diametrical compression/tensile, and shear tests. The shear test was identified as the most sensitive and repeatable, because it produced a sharp failure along a predetermined surface and showed a linear relationship between cake strength and the amount of water absorbed before drying. The excerpt does not provide the requested lactose RH sequence (0, 30, 58, 85%), a 48-hour flow-rate index or shear dataset, sodium chloride’s 75% DRH, numerical DEM evaporation slopes or angle-of-repose results, or a comparison between a controlled-RH FT4 experiment and DEM. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a controlled-humidity lactose experiment using coarse and fine alpha-lactose blends containing 0%, 5%, 10%, or 20% fine lactose. Samples were conditioned for 48 h at 0%, 30%, 58%, and 85% RH at 25 ± 1 °C. Flowability was measured with an FT4 Powder Rheometer using dynamic, permeability, and shear-cell tests; reported flow parameters included normalized basic flow energy, Flow Rate Index (FRI), and specific energy. FRI was defined as the ratio of flow energy at blade speeds of 10 and 100 mm/s. Measurements were repeated three times, but the excerpt does not provide numerical FRI or shear results. It reports that flow and dispersion deteriorated after 85% RH conditioning and improved after 58% RH conditioning; caking was observed at 85% RH. The excerpt contains no information about NaCl deliquescence relative humidity (75%), sucrose bridge caking, DEM evaporation-slope modeling, angle-of-repose tests, or comparison between DEM and experiments. It therefore supports discussion of the controlled-RH FT4 protocol and qualitative outcomes only. It also does not indicate that the FT4 measurements were validated against DEM; these appear to be separate topics or studies rather than a combined validation within Lu et al.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a controlled-relative-humidity accelerated caking experiment for sucrose, not lactose, NaCl, DEM, or FT4 validation. A forced-convection device controlled temperature, RH, airflow, and normal stress; RH was adjustable from 5% to 93% at 25 °C, with a maximum flowrate of 15 NL/min. Sucrose crystals (315–400 µm) were humidified at 89.5% RH and 25 °C, explicitly above the deliquescence relative humidity, under 10 kPa normal stress and 15 NL/min airflow. Humidification lasted 40 minutes to 10 hours, producing water contents from 0.19% to 2.46%. Samples were then dried at 30% RH and 25 °C under the same stress and flow conditions, inducing drying and recrystallization; final water content was approximately 0.041% ± 0.01%. Caking was measured using uniaxial compression, diametrical compression, and shear tests. In the shear test, a defined fracture surface formed between two cells, and shear stress increased linearly until failure. For sucrose, maximum stress and energy generally increased with increasing water uptake before drying in the uniaxial and shear tests, while diametrical compression showed no significant response increase. The excerpt supplies no lactose RH series (0/30/58/85), NaCl DRH value, DEM evaporation-slope or repose-angle comparison, numerical model validation, or evidence that controlled-RH FT4 results were validated with DEM in the same study.

contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How do physics-based simulations represent humidity and moisture effects on fine-powder flow: liquid (capillary) bridge force models in DEM (Willett, Rabinovich, Lian, pendular regime), relative-humidity-dependent cohesion, hygroscopic salts such as NaCl and BaCl2 with deliquescence and caking by solid bridges, and moisture sorption kinetics? Which open-source DEM codes implement capillary forces (LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, Yade, MercuryDPM)? How have these models been validated against shear-cell, angle-of-repose or flow-rate measurements at controlled humidity, and could they model an experiment in which a powder is dosed before and after exposure to humid air?

# Humidity-aware DEM for an auger powder doser

**The modeling distinction is between liquid already present at contacts and water supplied as vapor.** Pendular-bridge DEM can predict the forces exerted by an assigned small liquid volume. It does not, by itself, determine whether humid air produces that volume, how quickly water reaches powder inside a reservoir, or whether a dissolved salt subsequently recrystallizes into a persistent bond. Those require a sorption/transport and, for salts, a phase-change model. A dry SJKR-cohesion model that reproduces salt’s mass per revolution is therefore a valuable baseline, but not evidence that its cohesion parameter represents moisture or will transfer across humidity histories. (gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 5-7, samain2019characterizationofcaking pages 1-5, coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34)

## Contact physics and humidity

In the **pendular regime**, isolated menisci connect particle pairs. A DEM contact law combines surface-tension and Laplace-pressure attraction, with force depending on separation, particle radii, surface tension, contact angle and bridge volume; the force persists after particles lose mechanical contact and vanishes at bridge rupture. A commonly used small-separation pull-off scale is approximately \(2\pi R_*\gamma\cos\theta\), where \(R_*\) is an effective radius; rupture distance scales approximately as \(V_b^{1/3}\), with contact-angle corrections. The simplified Willett approximation supplies a separation-dependent force; classical Willett is a more detailed fit. Lian gives a useful rupture-distance approximation. Rabinovich’s minimum-energy expression is another choice, but Gabrieli and colleagues note Lambert’s objection that adding a separate adhesion term to that energy-derived force can double-count it. These alternatives should be benchmarked with the same radius and volume conventions before interpreting fitted parameters physically. Isolated-pair laws cease to be sufficient when liquid bridges merge or liquid redistributes substantially. (schwarze2013rheologyofweakly pages 5-6, coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 18-20, bagheri2025discreteelementsimulations pages 5-9, gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 7-9)

**Relative humidity (RH) is not bridge volume.** For vapor-condensed water, the Kelvin relation links equilibrium meniscus curvature and capillary pressure to water activity, approximately \(p_c=-(RT/V_w)\ln(\mathrm{RH})\) when RH is expressed as a fraction, subject to curvature and sign conventions. One must additionally determine *which contacts contain water*, their accessible geometry and roughness, and their liquid volumes. At the micro-/millimetre scale, wet-granular simulations often prescribe bridge volume instead and calculate capillary pressure from it—an importantly different boundary condition. An empirical \(F_{\rm adh}(\mathrm{RH})\) or RH-dependent SJKR energy is a defensible **effective** model for rapid screening, but it cannot identify a unique liquid-bridge volume, sorption rate or salt phase from dosing data alone. Electrostatics may also change with RH, so an observed flow change need not be capillary-only. (gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 5-7, janewska2024simulatingcapillaryforce pages 5-9, lu2017theeffectsof pages 3-7, lu2017theeffectsof pages 7-9)

For **NaCl**, the approximate deliquescence RH is **75%** for sufficiently large crystals under the conditions discussed by Hird and Bolton. Above deliquescence, a salt-solution film or bridge—not pure-water wetting of an inert sphere—can form; upon drying, dissolution and recrystallization can leave *solid bridges*. Thus the before/after-drying force can increase even when the final water content falls. Samain and colleagues demonstrated this sequence explicitly in a different crystalline material, sucrose: crystals were humidified at 89.5% RH, 25 °C, then dried at 30% RH; shear-measured cake strength increased with water taken up before drying. Their sucrose threshold, 85% RH, must **not** be assigned to NaCl or BaCl₂. I did not establish a reliable BaCl₂ deliquescence threshold or hydrate-transition conditions from the retrieved evidence; measure or obtain phase-specific data for the supplied BaCl₂ grade rather than borrowing NaCl’s threshold. Hygroscopic polymers, flour and metal powders likewise need separate sorption and surface-chemistry characterization. (hird2016migrationofsodium pages 2-4, samain2019characterizationofcaking pages 1-5, samain2019characterizationofcaking pages 7-11)

To represent **exposure duration**, measure adsorption *and desorption* mass-versus-time curves at controlled temperature and RH, for both a thin sample and the actual filled reservoir. A practical reduced model uses an equilibrium sorption isotherm \(w_{\rm eq}(\mathrm{RH},T)\), an uptake law such as \(dw/dt=k[w_{\rm eq}-w]\), and, when needed, vapor diffusion through the bed or particle interiors. Map local \(w\) to bridge occupancy/volume and to independently evolving solid-bond fraction or strength. Treat adsorption, drying and repeated RH cycles separately; the first-order law is an approximation to test against measured kinetics, not a property supplied by a standard capillary contact law. DEM with shrinking bridge volumes has reproduced evaporation-driven granular-slope evolution, but that study prescribed an evaporation law and accelerated it heavily to make the mechanical simulation feasible—it did not solve arbitrary ambient-RH sorption in a doser. (gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 1-3, gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 5-7, gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 20-24, gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 18-20)

For your existing LIGGGHTS outlet model, adding a verified liquid-bridge contact law is a smaller change than changing simulators. Check the precise branch/version and wall-contact implementation; published LIGGGHTS Willett and wet-granulation implementations do not establish that your installation automatically transports vapor or creates bonds during idle exposure. MercuryDPM offers a documented alternative for comparing simplified/classical Willett and Bagheri pair laws; its published examples are **particle-pair** demonstrations. The retrieved LAMMPS evidence supports a *custom* granular contact implementation, not the claim that atomistic simulations with explicit water constitute an off-the-shelf auger-scale DEM humidity model. Yade’s commonly described `CapillaryEngine`/imposed-suction workflow should be checked against the intended version’s documentation: direct implementation documentation and controlled-RH validation were not independently recovered here. (schwarze2013rheologyofweakly pages 5-6, kumar2021particlescalemodelingto pages 4-5, bagheri2025discreteelementsimulations pages 1-5, rhea2018multiphaseflowin pages 27-32)

## What has been validated?

- **Wet shear, with liquid deliberately added:** Badetti and colleagues obtained *quantitative* agreement between pendular-bridge DEM and rheometry of wet polystyrene beads after fixing interparticle friction from the dry material (approximately 0.09). Their controlled variable was added liquid content and applied stress, **not RH**. Their results also caution against treating bulk Mohr–Coulomb cohesion as a universal constant at low confining pressure. (badetti2018shearstrengthof pages 2-3, badetti2018shearstrengthof pages 1-2)
- **LIGGGHTS bridge force and bulk rheology:** Schwarze and colleagues checked their Willett implementation against two-sphere separation experiments using 13.6, 31.3 and 74.2 nL bridges. Their wet-granular rheometer simulation reproduced *trends* in apparent viscosity, but the authors did not claim a completed quantitative constitutive match to the bulk experiment. This is pair-force and added-liquid validation, not a humid-air dosing test. (schwarze2013rheologyofweakly pages 5-6, schwarze2013rheologyofweakly pages 6-8, schwarze2013rheologyofweakly pages 9-11)
- **Repose/slope during drying:** Gabrieli and colleagues compared an evaporating wet-glass-bead slope with DEM: the experimental initial wet slope was about 43°, versus about 28° for dry material; the simulated final upper and toe angles were about **35° and 21°**, comparable with experimental upper and toe regions of about **37° and 19°**. This supports the *mechanism* of weakening as bridges evaporate, but its initial water was added and evaporation was prescribed, not inferred from controlled-RH exposure. (gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 20-24, gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 18-20)
- **Controlled-RH powder flow, without matching DEM validation:** Lu and colleagues conditioned lactose blends for **48 h at 0%, 30%, 58% and 85% RH**, then measured FT4 dynamic-flow, permeability and shear responses. Flow was relatively good at intermediate RH and deteriorated at 85% RH; the change depended on fines fraction and was not simply monotonic. Their measured FT4 dynamic-property panels provide useful experimental comparators, **not** a validation of a humidity-aware DEM contact law. Sucrose humidity-cycle caking and shear-strength experiments likewise validate the importance of drying history, not an auger simulation. I did not find an equally substantiated *controlled-RH, same-powder* demonstration jointly matching DEM shear cell, repose and dosing/discharge across all conditions. (lu2017theeffectsof pages 1-3, lu2017theeffectsof pages 7-9, lu2017theeffectsof media 903ed815, lu2017theeffectsof media d3ea6a04, samain2019characterizationofcaking pages 7-11)

## A tractable pre-/post-exposure dosing study

1. **Control and measure the material state.** Split each powder lot into dry/control, humid-exposed, and humid-then-redried aliquots. Log actual RH and temperature *inside or immediately at the reservoir*, exposure duration, initial fill/packing, sample mass gain or loss, and delay before each test. Include levels below and across NaCl’s approximate threshold, with suitable containment and material-specific limits; determine BaCl₂ transitions independently. Measure an uptake/desorption time course rather than assuming that the reservoir equilibrates in the same time as a thin test sample. (hird2016migrationofsodium pages 2-4, gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 5-7, samain2019characterizationofcaking pages 7-11)
2. **Collect matched fingerprints and independent tests.** Randomize replicate runs across tilt, speed, fill level and tap setting; record the *distribution* of mass per revolution, tap-released mass, afterflow and zero-flow increments, including complete blockages. At the same conditioning state, measure the proposed ASTM D7891 FT4 and D6773 ring-shear responses, B213/B964 funnel flow or no-flow, B212/B527 bulk/tap densities, repose, B214/B822 size distributions, and loss on drying. Document sample preparation and consolidation: comparisons of FT4 and Schulze-family shear devices can differ systematically because pre-shearing differs. Hall/Carney no-flow is an informative outcome, not missing data. (shi2018effectofparticle pages 1-2, lu2017theeffectsof pages 1-3)
3. **Calibrate hierarchically.** First constrain dry size distribution, packing, particle–particle and PLA/PETG-wall sliding/rolling friction, restitution and geometry with dry tests; use the supplied 105 mg/revolution salt match as an *out-of-sample baseline check* where possible. Then infer an effective humidity-dependent force, or explicit bridge occupancy/volume and rupture law if independently measured sorption supports them. Add persistent solid bonds for humid-then-dried salt only if that history requires them. Fit a joint likelihood for continuous mass and time outputs, tap response, and binomial/sequence-aware no-flow events; include balance noise, run-to-run packing and simulator discrepancy. Repose alone cannot separate friction, rolling resistance and adhesion: published calibration examples produce different parameter sets across slump and hopper tests. Report posterior *effective parameters and correlations*, not an unjustified unique microscopic surface energy. (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34, shi2018effectofparticle pages 1-2, gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 18-20)
4. **Spend DEM runs on discrimination, not brute-force posterior sampling.** At the stated **26–30 CPU-min per simulated revolution**, screen sensitivity and fit an uncertainty-aware surrogate using selected tilt/speed/RH-history conditions, then run direct DEM checks at posterior extremes and held-out conditions. Advance the sorption/solid-bond state on the measured exposure-time scale and use DEM for the comparatively short dispensing/tapping intervals; explicitly model the 3 mm outlet and particle–printed-wall interactions. A repeatable failure of a liquid-only model to predict the redried sample’s no-flow rate or tap response would be evidence to test a caking/bond-history model, **not** proof of a particular salt bridge chemistry. (samain2019characterizationofcaking pages 1-5, gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 20-24, coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34)
5. **Test transfer to additive-manufacturing spreading separately.** Carry the *posterior distribution* of contact and size parameters into a recoater/roller geometry and measure deposited-layer mass or density, coverage/voids and surface roughness at controlled RH and spreading speed. Dosing from an auger, gravity funnel flow and formation of a thin moving powder bed impose different stresses and boundaries; even a well-matched dosing fingerprint does not alone validate spreadability. Published spreading work assesses layer packing and nonuniformity directly rather than identifying layer quality from repose alone. (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, lee2019quantificationofpowder pages 21-28, alchikhsulaiman2020powderspreadingand pages 63-66)

**Bottom line:** A before/after humid-air dosing experiment is feasible now as an experimentally conditioned, state-dependent DEM comparison. Predicting its *time course* or irreversible salt caking requires measured sorption/phase history and new coupling; none of the wet-bridge implementations established here should be treated as a ready-made, validated RH-to-NaCl/BaCl₂-cake-to-auger-to-powder-bed pipeline. (gabrieli2012micromechanicalmodellingof pages 5-7, bagheri2025discreteelementsimulations pages 1-5, samain2019characterizationofcaking pages 1-5, lu2017theeffectsof pages 1-3)

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How do physics-based simulations represent humidity and moisture effects on fine-powder flow: liquid (capillary) bridge force models in DEM (Willett, Rabinovich, Lian, pendular regime), relative-humidity-dependent cohesion, hygroscopic salts such as NaCl and BaCl2 with deliquescence and caking by solid bridges, and moisture sorption kinetics? Which open-source DEM codes implement capillary forces (LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS, Yade, MercuryDPM)? How have these models been validated against shear-cell, angle-of-repose or flow-rate measurements at controlled humidity, and could they model an experiment in which a powder is dosed before and after exposure to humid air?
